title: Spec-Patent Trawler — overview and definition
body:
Public edition. Public innovation-method knowledge, fact-checked reference. A spec-patent trawler is a system that sweeps through existing files, records, and databases, pulls out working ideas and mechanisms, and recombines them into brand-new specification drafts. It does not copy. It harvests patterns: a latch from a toolbox record, a sensor trick from a weather-station record, a folding trick from a tent record, and fuses them into an original invention that never existed before.

The trawler runs three moves on every haul. Mix-and-match blends two or more records into hybrids. Further-development takes one strong record and grows it — bigger scope, better materials, smarter control. Simple-version reduction strips a complex record down to its cheapest working core. Every output is a Signature-original draft: an original specification written fresh, never a reworded copy of a real patent.

This database is the trawler's own instruction book. It documents the public, long-established invention methods the trawler is allowed to use, the pipeline it runs, and the rules that keep every output original.
capabilities: Trawl files and databases for reusable mechanisms and patterns
Mix-and-match records into original hybrid invention drafts
Develop a strong record further into a larger or smarter version
Reduce a complex record to its cheapest working simple version
Score and rank drafts so only the best feed the spec pipeline

title: Morphological analysis — the mix-and-match grid
body:
Public edition. Public innovation-method knowledge, fact-checked reference. Morphological analysis is a real, documented invention method created by astronomer Fritz Zwicky in the 1940s and 1950s. The method is simple: break a problem into its independent parameters, list every known option for each parameter in a grid, then systematically combine one option from each column. Every cell combination is a candidate invention.

Zwicky used it for jet propulsion research, but the grid works anywhere. A lamp becomes columns for power source, housing shape, mounting, and control; picking one option per column generates dozens of lamp concepts, most never built before. The spec-patent trawler uses exactly this move when it mixes records: each record is a column of options, and the trawler walks the grid looking for combinations that work and that nobody has filed.

The discipline matters as much as the creativity. The grid forces completeness — every parameter gets considered, so the trawler does not keep re-inventing the same three combinations. It also forces honesty: a combination that fails physically gets marked as failed, not filed.
capabilities: Decompose any device into independent parameter columns
List all known options per parameter from trawled records
Generate candidate inventions from full column combinations
Mark physically impossible combinations as rejected, not filed
Feed surviving combinations into draft scoring

title: SCAMPER — seven verbs for transforming a record
body:
Public edition. Public innovation-method knowledge, fact-checked reference. SCAMPER is a documented creativity checklist published by Bob Eberle in 1971, built on Alex Osborn's earlier brainstorming work. Each letter is a verb to apply to an existing product or record: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify (also magnify or minify), Put to another use, Eliminate, Reverse.

The trawler applies SCAMPER to every record it hauls in. Substitute swaps the power source. Combine merges two records into one device. Adapt borrows a mechanism from an unrelated field. Modify scales a part up or down. Put to another use finds a second job for the device. Eliminate deletes the most expensive part and asks whether it still works. Reverse flips the process backward. Each verb produces a candidate draft, and the trawler scores them.

SCAMPER's strength is that it never stares at a blank page. It starts from something real — a trawled record — and transforms it step by step, so every output has a traceable lineage back to its parents and every change is a deliberate, describable engineering decision.
capabilities: Apply seven transformation verbs to any trawled record
Substitute materials, power sources, or mechanisms
Combine two records into a single hybrid device
Eliminate the costliest part and re-test function
Reverse a process to find the mirror-image invention

title: TRIZ — solving contradictions instead of compromising
body:
Public edition. Public innovation-method knowledge, fact-checked reference. TRIZ is a real, documented invention methodology developed by Soviet engineer Genrich Altshuller, who studied hundreds of thousands of patents starting in the 1940s. Its core finding: most hard inventions are contradictions — you want a part stronger AND lighter, faster AND more accurate. TRIZ says do not compromise; resolve the contradiction with one of 40 inventive principles, such as segmentation, asymmetry, or nesting.

The trawler uses TRIZ when a mixed draft hits a wall: the hybrid wants two things that fight each other. Instead of watering both down, the trawler looks up the contradiction pair and applies the suggested principles. Stronger-but-lighter resolves to hollow structures or composites. Faster-but-accurate resolves to staging or feedback loops.

Altshuller's work is public, published, and taught worldwide, which makes it safe trawler fuel: a method, not a patented device. The trawler never lifts a patented solution; it applies the public contradiction-solving method to its own original drafts.
capabilities: Detect contradiction pairs in a draft (stronger vs lighter, etc.)
Look up applicable inventive principles for the pair
Apply segmentation, asymmetry, nesting, or feedback to resolve
Reject compromise solutions that weaken both sides
Document which principle resolved which contradiction

title: Simple-version reduction — the cheapest working core
body:
Public edition. Public innovation-method knowledge, fact-checked reference. Making simple versions is a real, documented engineering discipline. The KISS principle ("keep it simple, stupid"), coined as a US Navy design note in 1960, demands that systems work without complex failure chains. The minimum viable product method, popularized in lean-startup literature, ships the smallest thing that still solves the problem and learns from it.

The trawler's simple-version move follows a fixed procedure. List every feature of the parent record. Rank each by how much function the device loses if the feature is deleted. Delete from the bottom until the next deletion would break the core job. What remains is the simple version: cheaper to build, easier to repair, faster to test. A solar lantern with Bluetooth, GPS, and a speaker becomes a solar lantern with a switch — same light, a tenth of the cost.

Simple versions are often the most fileable drafts. Complexity is where prior art hides; the stripped core is where originality shows. The trawler always generates the simple version alongside the full version and scores both.
capabilities: Rank every feature by function lost if deleted
Strip features bottom-up until the core job would break
Produce the cheapest working core as a separate draft
Score simple and full versions independently
Prefer the simple version when scores tie

title: Further development — growing a record past its parents
body:
Public edition. Public innovation-method knowledge, fact-checked reference. Further development is the oldest invention move there is: take something that works and grow it. Iterative design — build, test, improve, repeat — is documented engineering practice across every industry, from the Wright brothers' wind-tunnel cycles to modern software sprints. The trawler formalizes it into a draft-generation move.

The procedure: pick a strong parent record. Identify its three limits — what it cannot do, where it breaks, who it cannot serve. Attack each limit in turn. A hand-crank flashlight's limits are arm fatigue, low brightness, and dead batteries in storage; further development adds a flywheel, swaps in efficient LEDs, and adds a trickle solar cell. Each attack must be describable as an engineering change with a test.

The rule that keeps this honest: further development must change the record, not reword it. If the "new" draft does the same job the same way with the same parts, it is not a draft — it is a copy, and the trawler rejects it. Growth must be measurable in function, scope, or users served.
capabilities: Identify a parent record and its three hard limits
Attack each limit with a describable engineering change
Require a test for every claimed improvement
Reject drafts that do the same job the same way
Measure growth in function, scope, or users served

title: Prior-art trawling — harvesting without copying
body:
Public edition. Public innovation-method knowledge, fact-checked reference. Patent searching is real, public, and encouraged: patent offices worldwide publish granted patents and applications precisely so inventors can see what exists. The trawler treats all of his own files and databases the same way — a private prior-art library to search before drafting.

The harvest protocol has three gates. First, relevance: the record must contain a mechanism, material, or method usable in a new combination — pure descriptions with no working content are skipped. Second, lineage: every harvested element is tagged with its source record id, so the draft's family tree is complete. Third, the originality gate: the final draft must differ in at least one functional element from every parent; a draft that reassembles parents unchanged is rejected as a copy.

This is what separates trawling from plagiarism. Plagiarism hides its sources and changes the words. Trawling declares its sources and changes the machine. The lineage tags are the proof: anyone can follow a draft back to its parents and see exactly what was added, removed, or transformed.
capabilities: Search the private prior-art library before drafting
Tag every harvested element with its source record id
Require at least one functional difference from every parent
Reject drafts that reassemble parents unchanged
Publish the full lineage with every draft

title: The trawler pipeline — harvest, mix, draft, score
body:
Public edition. Process record for the trawler's own operation. The trawler runs a four-stage pipeline, and every draft that reaches the spec queue has passed all four.

Stage one, harvest: sweep the connected files and databases, pull candidate records, tag each element with its source. Stage two, mix: apply the mix-and-match grid, SCAMPER verbs, and TRIZ contradiction-solving to generate candidate drafts — hybrids, further developments, and simple versions. Stage three, draft: write each surviving candidate as a full specification — problem, solution, detailed description, claims-style statements, and a simple-version embodiment. Stage four, score: rank every draft on novelty, function, buildability, and simplicity, and keep only the drafts that clear the bar.

The pipeline is throttled and self-regulating. It stops requesting new harvests when the draft queue is full, it deduplicates against every draft already filed, and it halts entirely if the novelty scores collapse — a sign the well is dry and the trawler should rest rather than pad the queue with weak drafts.
capabilities: Harvest candidate records with full source tagging
Mix candidates via grid, SCAMPER, and TRIZ moves
Write survivors as full specifications with claims-style text
Score drafts on novelty, function, buildability, simplicity
Halt when novelty collapses instead of padding the queue

title: Draft scoring — ranking candidates fairly
body:
Public edition. Process record for the trawler's own operation. Scoring is what keeps the trawler honest. Every draft gets four numbers, each zero to one hundred. Novelty: how functionally different it is from its parents and from everything already filed — measured, not guessed, by feature-set distance. Function: does it actually do the job it claims, and can the mechanism be described without hand-waving. Buildability: could a skilled person build it from the description with ordinary tools and materials. Simplicity: fewer parts and fewer failure modes score higher.

The weights are fixed: novelty 35, function 30, buildability 20, simplicity 15. The bar is 60 out of 100 to reach the spec queue. Drafts below the bar are not deleted — they are parked with their scores, because a parked draft can become a parent for a future mix that pushes it over the line.

Scoring is deterministic and recorded. Every draft carries its four numbers and the reasons behind them, so a human reviewer can audit any decision the trawler made. No black-box rejections, no mystery promotions.
capabilities: Score every draft on novelty, function, buildability, simplicity
Measure novelty by feature-set distance, never by gut feel
Apply fixed weights: 35 / 30 / 20 / 15
Park sub-bar drafts with scores for future mixing
Record all scores and reasons for human audit

title: Bisociation — stealing fire from unrelated fields
body:
Public edition. Public innovation-method knowledge, fact-checked reference. Bisociation is a real term from Arthur Koestler's 1964 book The Act of Creation: creativity happens when two unrelated frames of reference collide. The printing press came from a wine press plus movable type. Velcro came from burrs plus textiles. The trawler runs bisociation deliberately instead of waiting for accidents.

The move: take a mechanism that works perfectly in field A and drop it into field B where nobody uses it. A kitchen whisk's wire loops become a paint mixer. A ratchet from a socket wrench becomes a one-way hinge on a gate. A camera's aperture iris becomes an adjustable vent. The mechanism is proven; only the context is new, and the new context is where the originality lives.

The trawler keeps a mechanism catalog stripped of context — just the motion, the force path, the geometry — and a domain catalog of unsolved small problems. Bisociation is matching one against the other. The catalog is the trawler's richest fuel because every entry is a proven working thing looking for a second job.
capabilities: Maintain a context-free catalog of proven mechanisms
Maintain a catalog of unsolved small problems by domain
Match mechanisms against problems in unrelated domains
Verify the mechanism still works in the new context
Document the parent mechanism and the new domain in lineage

title: Reverse engineering as inspiration — learning from teardown
body:
Public edition. Public innovation-method knowledge, fact-checked reference. Reverse engineering — taking a product apart to understand how it works — is a real, legal, and widely practiced engineering method when applied to products you own and ideas you re-implement yourself. Entire industries, from compatible printer cartridges to open hardware, were built on careful teardown and clean-room re-implementation.

The trawler's teardown protocol is strict. Disassemble the parent record conceptually: list every part, every joint, every force path. Understand why each part is shaped the way it is — the function behind the form. Then close the teardown notes and design fresh from the functions, not from the shapes. The new draft must achieve the same functions with a different arrangement; if the arrangement is identical, it is a copy and it is rejected.

The output of a teardown is understanding, not a blueprint. The trawler files the understanding — "this latch works because the spring preloads past center" — and that principle becomes trawler fuel for entirely different devices. Principles travel; blueprints do not.
capabilities: Teardown a parent record into parts, joints, and force paths
Extract the function behind every form
Design fresh from functions, never from shapes
Reject drafts whose arrangement matches the parent
File principles as reusable trawler fuel

title: From draft to spec — writing claims-style descriptions
body:
Public edition. Process record for the trawler's own operation. A trawler draft is not finished until it reads like a real specification: clear enough that a skilled person could build the thing. The trawler writes five sections for every draft.

One, the problem: what is broken, missing, or too expensive today, stated plainly. Two, the solution: what the invention is and what it does, in one paragraph. Three, the detailed description: how it is built, part by part, with materials and dimensions where they matter. Four, claims-style statements: numbered sentences starting "The invention comprises..." that pin down exactly what is new — written in the style of patent claims but labeled as draft claims, never filed language. Five, the simple version: the stripped embodiment, proving the idea survives simplification.

Every draft is labeled Signature-original and carries its full lineage: parent records, mix method used, scores, and the trawler run that produced it. The label is a promise — this is his original invention, inspired by his own records, never a reworded copy of anyone's patent.
capabilities: Write the problem in plain, specific language
Describe the build part by part with materials
Pin down novelty in numbered claims-style statements
Include the simple-version embodiment for every draft
Label every draft Signature-original with full lineage
